docs.text: Frequently Asked Questions General & Environment "What Python version is required?" SNEPPX-Alg requires Python 3.9+ (tested on Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12). "Does SNEPPX-Alg require a GPU or CUDA?" No. All core tensor operations, autograd, optimizers, neural layers, and quantization algorithms run on pure CPU with the NumPy-backed engine. GPU acceleration (CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan) is strictly opt-in. "How do I run tests safely on a local CPU machine?" Run tests per-file using pytest without cache provider: $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" python -m pytest tests/python/test_tensor.py -q -p no:cacheprovider Never execute the entire tests/ directory in a single command on memory-constrained machines, and skip GPU/LLM tests ( test_llama_models.py , test_cuda.py ). "What is the difference between sx.functional and F ?" sx.functional is reserved by the core autograd engine for forward/reverse mode derivatives ( jvp , vjp ). For neural network activations and loss functions, import F instead: from SneppX_ALG import F # F.relu, F.mse_loss, F.cross_entropy, F.layer_norm "Can I migrate models from PyTorch?" Yes. SNEPPX-Alg supports state_dict weight loading and provides functional and module APIs deliberately aligned with standard deep learning semantics. See migration/from_pytorch.md . Installation & Build "mkdocs build fails — doxygen: command not found " Install Doxygen 1.9+ (see docs/api/index.md ). On Windows: vcpkg install doxygen ; on Linux: sudo apt-get install doxygen graphviz . "CMake cannot find a C/C++ compiler on Windows" Install Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload (includes MSVC 19.44 and MASM), or run from Developer PowerShell so cl.exe / ml64 are on PATH : cmake -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build --config Release cd build && ctest -C Release --output-on-failure "ninja.exe crashes with heap corruption" The Kitware dev-build Ninja in some environments can be unstable. Use the repo-root ninja.exe (Ninja ≥ 1.12), or fall back to the Visual Studio generator: cmake -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" . Python API "ImportError: cannot import name 'X' from 'SneppX_ALG'" Top-level from SneppX_ALG import * re-exports primary symbols ( Tensor , F , nn , optim ). Other tools live under interface_bindings and require setting PYTHONPATH : $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" from SneppX_ALG import Tensor, F, Linear, AdamW from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.tokenizer import Tokenizer from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.data_loader import DataLoader from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.generation import GenerationConfig, generate "RuntimeError: C backend not available" This indicates compiled extension binaries ( _SNEPPX_c*.pyd or .so ) were not linked. The pure-Python/NumPy fallback handles tensors and basic modules seamlessly without needing C compilation: import SneppX_ALG as s print(s._HAS_C_BACKEND) # False = Pure-Python mode; True = Native C acceleration "CUDA not available" If you do not have an NVIDIA GPU, keep SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=OFF (the default). The engine operates natively in CPU mode. Quantization "quantize OOM / runs forever on a 7B model" Use per-channel or per-group INT8 ( QuantGranularity.PER_CHANNEL , group size 128). For weights-only quantization (W8A16), prefer QuantizedLinear.from_float over whole-tensor paths. On CPU, wrap the loop in quantize_model_weights(...) which skips lm_head / embed_tokens by default. "INT4 weights decode incorrectly" Ensure the quantizer and dequantizer specify the exact n (total element count): dequantize_int4_sym(qw, scale, n) requires the original element count rather than packed byte size. Distributed Training "Training hangs after init_process_group" On CPU machines without NCCL, verify that every rank specifies matching MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT : $env:MASTER_ADDR="127.0.0.1"; $env:MASTER_PORT="29500" $env:WORLD_SIZE=2; $env:RANK=0; $env:LOCAL_RANK=0 Security "How do I report a security vulnerability?" See repository security policy . Do not open public issues for security vulnerabilities — report them privately via GitHub Security Advisories or email algoSNEPPX@gmail.com . Still stuck? Read Getting Started for quick setup. Read Installation Guide for deep build notes. Open an issue at the SneppX Issue Tracker .

docs.text: Glossary Term Definition ARC Adversarial Robustness Core -- three-layer defense pipeline (input guard, gradient obfuscation, output verifier + attack simulation) ARI Abstract Representation Intermediate -- intermediate representation used by NPE compilers ASLR Address Space Layout Randomization -- heap entropy via randomized memory allocation Autodiff Automatic differentiation -- tape-based reverse-mode gradient computation BDFL Benevolent Dictator For Life -- project governance model Blelloch Tree-based parallel prefix scan algorithm used by HSS for O(log n) state updates BPE Byte-Pair Encoding -- subword tokenization algorithm C&W Carlini-Wagner -- optimization-based adversarial attack Canary Stack-based overflow detection value with generation counter cuBLAS NVIDIA's CUDA Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms library CUDA NVIDIA's parallel computing platform, used for GPU-accelerated optimizer DCE Dead Code Elimination -- JIT pass that removes NOPs and unused instructions FGSM Fast Gradient Sign Method -- single-step adversarial attack FM Federated Memory -- multi-node memory banks with trust-weighted sync + NCCL bridge HSS Hierarchical State Space -- multi-layer SSM with O(n log n) Blelloch parallel scan JIT Just-In-Time compilation -- runtime program optimization pipeline (DCE -> constant fold -> fuse -> compile) KV-Cache Key-Value Cache -- cached attention keys/values for autoregressive generation MHA Multi-Head Attention -- attention with multiple parallel heads MLP Gater Learned MLP-based router for SER (2-layer MLP replacing linear router) MoE Mixture of Experts -- sparse routing with top-k expert activation NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library -- multi-GPU synchronization NPE Neural Program Executor -- 16-register VM with 15+ opcodes + JIT pipeline PGD Projected Gradient Descent -- iterative adversarial attack RoPE Rotary Position Embedding -- relative position encoding for attention RNG Random Number Generator -- secure entropy source SER Sparse Expert Routing -- MoE layer with learned gating (linear or MLP) SSM State Space Model -- sequence model with latent state evolution ZKP Zero-Knowledge Proof -- cryptographic proof without revealing inputs ZOH Zero-Order Hold -- discretization method for continuous-time SSMs

docs.text: Good First Issues — sneppx-alg New to the codebase? This page lists approachable, well-scoped tasks that are a great way to make your first contribution. Each one is labeled good first issue on GitHub. How to pick one Browse the open good-first-issue list . Pick something that matches your skills (Python, C, docs, tests). Comment "I'd like to work on this" so maintainers can assign it to you. Fork, branch, implement, test, open a PR. Beginner-friendly areas Python bindings ( bindings/python/SneppX_ALG/ ) Add unit tests for an untested module (see tests/python/ for the pattern). Add a new nn module or optim optimizer following the existing wrappers. Improve docstrings / type hints. Documentation ( docs/ ) Fix typos, clarify build instructions, add examples. Add a tutorial (see docs/tutorials/ for the format). Improve the API reference ( docs/api/python.md ). Tests ( tests/python/ ) Add edge-case tests for existing ops. Add regression tests for fixed bugs. Benchmarks ( benchmarks/ , tests/benchmark/ ) Add a new benchmark for an op not yet covered. Update docs/benchmarks.md with fresh numbers. Before you start Read CONTRIBUTING.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . Build and run one test to confirm your environment works: powershell $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" python -m pytest tests/python/test_tensor.py -q -p no:cacheprovider Follow the commit-message convention: <area>: <description> (e.g. optim: add load_state_dict to SparseAdam ). Getting help 💬 Discussions — Q&A and ideas. 🐛 Issues — bugs and feature requests. 📚 Contributor Tiers — the full contribution ladder. Not sure where to start? Look for issues labeled good first issue or documentation . If none fit, open a discussion and ask — maintainers are happy to point you at something.

docs.text: SNEPPX-Algo Style Guide C Style Naming Functions : snake_case with SNEPPX_ prefix: SNEPPX_tensor_create Types : PascalCase with SNEPPX prefix: SNEPPXTensor Macros : UPPER_SNAKE_CASE : SNEPPX_FLOAT32 Constants : UPPER_SNAKE_CASE : MAX_TOKEN_LEN File-scope statics : s_ prefix: s_global_pool Formatting Indentation : 4 spaces, no tabs Line length : 100 characters max Braces : K&R style (opening brace on same line) Pointer alignment : Right ( int* p ) Spacing : One space after if , for , while , do , switch No space between function name and ( Space around binary operators No space around unary operators Headers Include guards: #ifndef SNEPPX_MODULE_NAME_H / #define SNEPPX_MODULE_NAME_H Standard headers first, then project headers, alphabetically Forward declarations preferred over includes when possible Example #ifndef SNEPPX_TENSOR_H #define SNEPPX_TENSOR_H #define SNEPPX_MAX_NDIM 8 typedef struct { float* data; size_t shape[SNEPPX_MAX_NDIM]; size_t ndim; size_t size; } SNEPPXTensor; SNEPPXTensor* SNEPPX_tensor_create(const size_t* shape, size_t ndim, SNEPPXDtype dtype); void SNEPPX_tensor_destroy(SNEPPXTensor* t); #endif Error Handling Return int (0 = success, nonzero = error) for operations Return NULL for failed allocations Check all allocation returns Never assert in production code paths Memory Always use SNEPPX_malloc / SNEPPX_free with size tracking Parameter order: output params before input params where possible Document ownership transfer C++ Style Used only for S2 obfuscation engine and pybind11 bindings. Namespace : SNEPPX Class names : PascalCase Method names : snake_case Variable names : snake_case Member variables : trailing underscore ( member_ ) RAII everywhere No exceptions in hot paths const correctness No RTTI No dynamic_cast Python Style PEP 8 compliant Line length: 88 columns (Black default) Formatter: Black (required) Type hints on all public functions Docstrings: Google style Tests use pytest Example from typing import Optional class Tensor: """Multi-dimensional array.""" def __init__(self, data: np.ndarray) -> None: self._data = data.astype(np.float32) def numpy(self) -> np.ndarray: return self._data.copy() Commit Messages component: Brief description in present tense Longer description explaining motivation and approach. Wrap at 72 characters. Prefix with component: tensor: , hss: , ser: , arc: , npe: , fm: , security: , build: , docs: , tests: , python: First line: max 72 chars Use imperative mood: "Fix", not "Fixed" GPG or Ed25519 commit signing required on main branch Documentation Style Markdown for all documentation files Code examples in fenced code blocks with language tag Tables for structured data Links use relative paths within the repository Naming Conventions Entity Convention Example C files snake_case tensor_ops.c C headers snake_case SNEPPX_tensor.h C functions snake_case SNEPPX_tensor_create C structs PascalCase SNEPPXTensor C enums PascalCase SNEPPXDtype C macros SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE SNEPPX_MAX_NDIM C++ classes PascalCase Tensor C++ methods snake_case tensor_create Python classes PascalCase Tensor Python functions snake_case from_numpy Directories snake_case kernel/tensor/ Commenting Standard See COMMENTING.md for the four-layer commenting standard: - Layer 1: File header blocks (WHAT/CONCEPT/ROLE/REFERENCES) - Layer 2: Concept blocks before non-obvious algorithms - Layer 3: Inline "why" comments - Layer 4: Doxygen @brief/@param/@return on every public SNEPPX_* function

docs.text: Vision & Thesis Elevator Pitch SNEPPX-Algo is the first open-source AI algorithm with cryptographic integrity -- neuro-symbolic execution where every inference is verifiable, every execution path is tamper-proof, and the model evolves on-device without compromising privacy. The algorithm protects itself so you can run it anywhere without trusting the host. The Problem Modern AI has a trust crisis: Closed models -- You don't know what the model is doing. You send data to an API and get back an answer. The computation is a black box. Open models can be tampered -- Even if the weights are public, nothing stops a malicious host from modifying the inference code, stealing the model, or poisoning the output. No verifiability -- There is no way to prove an inference was computed correctly without re-running it yourself. No on-device privacy -- Most "AI" requires sending your data to the cloud. On-device inference exists but lacks security guarantees. No open contribution model -- Open-source AI has no way to reward contributors or verify their contributions are honest. The Solution 1. Neuro-Symbolic Execution Combine neural network components (HSS, SER) with a symbolic program executor (NPE). The neural parts learn patterns; the symbolic parts verify logical correctness. The JIT pipeline optimizes hybrid programs at runtime. 2. Cryptographic Integrity Every inference produces a zero-knowledge proof that it was computed correctly. Users verify the proof without re-running the model. This is mathematically-guaranteed trust. Integrity proof : "This output is the correct result of model M on input X" Privacy preserving : The proof reveals nothing about the model weights Public verifiable : Anyone can check the proof with open-source verifier code 3. Self-Protecting Execution The algorithm encrypts its own memory, obfuscates its control flow, detects debuggers, and virtualizes critical functions. Running SNEPPX on an untrusted host is safer than running any other model anywhere. S0: All crypto primitives are constant-time, side-channel resistant S1: All allocations have guard pages, canaries, ASLR S2: Control flow is flattened, strings are encrypted, handlers are scrambled 4. On-Device First The core algorithm is designed to run on phones and edge devices, not just datacenter GPUs. Quantization-aware execution paths (INT8, FP8, AWQ, GPTQ) Sparse compute (MoE routes to only a few experts per token) Memory-efficient secure allocator (S1) No cloud dependency for inference 5. Federated Contribution Protocol Open-source AI needs an incentive and verification model. SNEPPX lets contributors train shards locally and submit cryptographically signed gradient contributions via the NCCL sync bridge. The protocol verifies contributions without seeing private data, turning the community into a distributed training network. Gradient contributions are signed with Ed25519 (S0) Contributions are aggregated via trust-weighted all-reduce (FM + NCCL) Contributors earn reputation scores based on verification 6. Formal Safety Guarantees The behavioral monitor (S3) enforces provable constraints at runtime -- not just "detect anomalies" but "prove the output satisfies safety bounds." Combined with the symbolic execution layer, every decision path is auditable. Design Principles Trust is mathematical, not organizational. Don't ask users to trust a company. Give them a proof. Security is foundational, not bolted on. Every layer from the allocator up is hardened. Open source is non-negotiable. The code, the proofs, the protocols -- all public. On-device is the default. Cloud is optional, not required. Contribute and verify. The community grows through cryptographically verified contributions. What Makes This Next-Gen Most "next-gen AI" is just bigger models trained on more GPUs. SNEPPX-Algo is next-gen because it rethinks the relationship between the algorithm and the user: From black box -> verifiable From trust-the-company -> trust-the-math From cloud-only -> on-device-first From centralized training -> federated contribution From reactive safety -> provable safety This isn't a better transformer. It's a fundamentally different category of AI system.

docs.text: Autograd Guide SNEPPX-Alg provides a full autograd engine with higher-order differentiation. !!! tip "See it happen" New to autograd? Start with the Autograd visualizer — type a scalar expression and watch gradients flow backwards through the graph. Basic usage import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor x = Tensor(np.array([2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True) y = (x * x).sum() y.backward() print(x.grad) # [4, 6] No-grad context from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.autograd import no_grad with no_grad(): z = x * 2 # no graph built Higher-order AD (create_graph) x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0]), requires_grad=True) y = (x ** 2).sum() y.backward(create_graph=True) # x.grad now has a graph attached g2 = (x.grad * x.grad).sum() g2.backward() Forward-mode (jvp) and reverse-mode (vjp) from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.autograd import jvp, vjp def f(x): return (x * x).sum() x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True) tangent = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])) jvp_result = jvp(f, x, tangent) Gradient checkpointing from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.grad_checkpoint import checkpoint def heavy(x): return x * x out = checkpoint(heavy, x) Supported ops with create_graph All 40+ ops support create_graph=True , including: Conv1d, Conv2d, Conv3d, Linear, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, BatchNorm, Embedding, all losses (MSE, CrossEntropy, BCE, etc.), all activations, MatMul, and more.

docs.text: Autograd visualizer Type a scalar expression, then watch the forward values appear and the backward pass propagate gradients through the graph. No installation — this runs entirely in your browser. ▶ Run Step backward Reset Presets: (a*b+c)*relu(a) square(a)+exp(b) tanh(ab)/(1+c²) sqrt|w|·log(eˣ+1) How to read it Each box is a node: the operator on top, its forward value in the middle, and the gradient ∂f/∂node above it once the backward pass reaches it. Edges point from inputs to their consumer, so the backward pass runs right-to-left. relu has a subgradient of 0 for negative inputs — that's why a gradient can vanish at a node. Supported syntax Element Examples Variables a , b , c , x , w Arithmetic + - * / ** and unary - Functions relu , exp , log , sqrt , square , tanh , abs Grouping ( ... ) Everything is scalar-valued, so the graph stays small and readable. For the real tensor engine, see the Autograd guide and the Cookbook .

docs.text: Build Instructions 1. Prerequisites Required: - CMake 3.16+ - C11/C++20 compiler (MSVC 19.44+, GCC 11+, Clang 14+) - Python 3.9+ (for bindings) Optional: - CUDA 12.0+ (GPU optimizer acceleration, SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON ) - Doxygen (API docs) 2. Quick Build (All Targets) This project is Ninja-based. Use the CMake presets (see CMakePresets.json ), which select the Ninja generator and write to per-config binary directories. Windows (MSVC): git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git cd sneppx-alg cmake --preset release cmake --build --preset release Linux/Mac (GCC/Clang): git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git cd sneppx-alg cmake --preset release cmake --build --preset release -j$(nproc) The release preset configures Release + LTO + tests; debug , asan , cuda , python , and minimal presets are also available. 3. Build Individual Targets Build into the active binary directory (e.g. build/release after the release preset), then reference targets: # Core kernel library cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_core_kernel # Architecture algorithms cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_architecture_layer # Security C library cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_security_c # Security C++ obfuscation cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_security_cpp # Python bindings cmake --build build/release --config Release --target _SNEPPX_c # CUDA kernels (requires CUDA SDK; use the `cuda` preset) cmake --preset cuda cmake --build --preset cuda --target neural_cuda_kernels 4. Build Options CMake Variable Default Description SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA OFF Enable CUDA kernel compilation SNEPPX_BUILD_PYTHON OFF Build Python bindings SNEPPX_BUILD_TESTS ON Build test executables SNEPPX_BUILD_EXAMPLES ON Build example programs SNEPPX_BUILD_VULKAN OFF Vulkan reference backend SNEPPX_BUILD_TPU OFF TPU reference backend SNEPPX_BUILD_HTTP OFF HTTP transport backend SNEPPX_BUILD_ZK OFF Zero-knowledge backend SNEPPX_ENABLE_ASAN OFF AddressSanitizer SNEPPX_ENABLE_UBSAN OFF UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer 5. Debug Build Use the debug preset (Ninja, Debug build type, tests+tools on): cmake --preset debug cmake --build --preset debug Debug builds disable optimization and enable assertions. Use -DSNEPPX_S1_SECURE_MEMORY=OFF for faster debug iteration. 6. Python Package Build # Editable install pip install -e . # With CUDA support pip install -e .[cuda] # Build wheel pip install build python -m build --wheel 7. Running Tests Run from the binary directory of the active preset (e.g. build/release ): # C tests cd build\release ctest -C Release --output-on-failure # Specific test ctest -C Release -R test_kyber # Sanitizer tests (Windows) powershell -File scripts/run_sanitizers.ps1 For Python-only tests (no build required): $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" python -m pytest tests/python/ -v 8. Common Issues Issue Fix cuda_runtime.h: No such file or directory Build without CUDA: -DSNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=OFF pybind11_add_module: Unknown CMake command Set pybind11_DIR or ensure FetchContent can reach GitHub LNK2001: unresolved external symbol Build neural_core_kernel and neural_security_c before _SNEPPX_c MSVC "no VLAs" Use calloc / free instead of stack-allocated VLAs __int128 undeclared on MSVC Guard with #ifndef NO_UINT128 (see x25519.c pattern) CreateProcess failed: The system cannot find the file specified. (MASM, Windows+Ninja) Use the stable Ninja 1.12+ (see scripts/ or repo root ninja.exe ); the Kitware dev Ninja in the venv can crash. The x64 MASM path ( ml64 ) is resolved automatically — no manual -DCMAKE_ASM_MASM_COMPILER needed. 9. Build Directories The project standardizes on CMake presets ( CMakePresets.json ), each using the Ninja generator and writing to a per-config binary directory. Prefer the presets: cmake --preset release → build/release cmake --preset debug → build/debug cmake --preset asan → build/asan cmake --preset cuda → build/cuda cmake --preset python → build/python cmake --preset minimal → build/min Avoid configuring the plain build/ directory with the presets; it is reserved for the legacy Visual Studio generator and is not Ninja-clean. See DEVELOPMENT.md for the full development workflow.

docs.text: The project standardizes on CMake presets ( CMakePresets.json ), each using the Ninja generator and writing to a per-config binary directory. Prefer the presets: cmake --preset release → build/release cmake --preset debug → build/debug cmake --preset asan → build/asan cmake --preset cuda → build/cuda cmake --preset python → build/python cmake --preset minimal → build/min Avoid configuring the plain build/ directory with the presets; it is reserved for the legacy Visual Studio generator and is not Ninja-clean. See DEVELOPMENT.md for the full development workflow.

docs.text: Code Walkthrough — The SNEPPX-Alg Pipeline This is the entry point for reading the SNEPPX-Alg source. It maps the five pipeline stages to their directories, header APIs, and per-module walkthroughs. The five-stage pipeline SNEPPX-Alg processes data through a fixed pipeline of five algorithm families. Each stage is a directory under algorithms/ and a public header under include/neural_core/architecture/ . Stage Name Header Directory Job 1 HSS — Hierarchical State Space hierarchical_state_space.h algorithms/hss/ Recurrent sequence modeling with a learnable state 2 SER — Sparse Expert Routing sparse_expert_routing.h algorithms/ser/ Mixture-of-experts gating, routing, and load balancing 3 ARC — Adversarial Robustness Certification adversarial_robustness_certification.h algorithms/arc/ Input guard, gradient obfuscation, output verification 4 NPE — Neural Programming Engine neural_programming_engine.h algorithms/npe/ 16-register neural VM with 32 opcodes and a JIT 5 FM — Fractal Memory Orchestrator fractal_memory_orchestrator.h algorithms/fm/ Distributed memory banks, sync, and federated state The pipeline is HSS → SER → ARC → NPE → FM: sequence features are extracted, sparsely routed through experts, adversarially hardened, executed as a differentiable program, then written into distributed memory. Shared foundations Every stage is built on three kernel subsystems (under include/neural_core/ and kernel/ ): multidimensional_tensor_engine.h — the SNEPPXTensor core used by every stage as its data type. automatic_differentiation_framework.h — the SNEPPXTape / SNEPPXVariable autodiff graph used for training. polymorphic_memory_allocator.h — the memory allocator used for allocation in each module's C sources. How each module is organized Every algorithm directory follows the same layout: algorithms/<stage>/core/*.c — CPU implementation of the stage. algorithms/<stage>/cuda/*.cu / *.cuh — CUDA kernels (built only when -DSNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON ). include/neural_core/architecture/<stage>.h — the public API. Per-module walkthroughs Module Walkthrough HSS walkthrough-hss.md SER walkthrough-ser.md ARC walkthrough-arc.md NPE walkthrough-npe.md FM walkthrough-fm.md Recommended reading order Start with walkthrough-hss.md — it introduces the tensor, layer, and train-graph patterns that the other four modules reuse. walkthrough-ser.md — adds gating and routing on top. walkthrough-arc.md — the security hardening stage. walkthrough-npe.md — a different execution model (a bytecode VM instead of plain tensor layers). walkthrough-fm.md — memory and distributed sync. Each walkthrough ends with a "minimal example" that compiles against the library, and the full public API of the module.

docs.text: Conv2d visualizer A convolution slides a small kernel over the input. Hover any output cell to see the exact window of input it read — and how stride and padding change the output size. padded input ∗ kernel = output stride 1 padding 0 🎲 Randomize The output-size formula out = floor((H + 2·pad − kernel) / stride) + 1 With H = 7 , kernel = 3 : stride pad output 1 0 5×5 1 1 7×7 2 0 3×3 2 1 4×4 SNEPPX-Alg's nn.Conv2d supports stride , padding , dilation , and groups , and its backward pass is exact (verified against finite differences in tests/python/test_conv2d_autograd.py ). import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn conv = nn.Conv2d(1, 4, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = Tensor(np.random.randn(1, 1, 7, 7).astype(np.float32)) print(conv(x).shape) # (1, 4, 7, 7) See also: Matmul visualizer · Autograd visualizer .

docs.text: Cookbook — common recipes Small, copy-pasteable recipes. Every Python block has a ▶ Run button that executes it in your browser (Pyodide + SneppX-Alg), so you can experiment without installing anything. Freeze a layer (stop gradients) import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn m = nn.Linear(4, 4) for p in m.parameters(): p.requires_grad_(False) trainable = sum(p.numel for p in m.parameters() if p.requires_grad) print("trainable elements:", trainable) Gradient clipping (global norm) import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.trainer_v2 import clip_grad_norm_ m = nn.Linear(4, 4) opt = optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=1e-2) x = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32)) y = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32)) loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(m(x), y) loss.backward() before = clip_grad_norm_(list(m.parameters()), max_norm=1.0) print("total grad norm before clipping:", round(float(before), 4)) Custom autograd Function import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import autograd class SquareFn(autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, x): ctx.save_for_backward(x=x) return Tensor(x.data ** 2, dtype=x.dtype) @staticmethod def backward(ctx, grad_output, create_graph=False): x = ctx.get_saved_tensor("x") return [Tensor(2 * x.data * grad_output.data, dtype=grad_output.dtype)] x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True) y = SquareFn.apply(x) y.sum().backward() print("forward:", y.data) print("gradient:", np.asarray(x.grad.data)) Matrix multiply with a linear layer import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor w = Tensor(np.random.randn(4, 4).astype(np.float32)) x = Tensor(np.random.randn(2, 4).astype(np.float32)) out = x @ w print("dtype / shape:", out.data.dtype, out.shape) Sparse embedding lookup import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import sparse indices = np.array([[0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2]]) values = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) sp = sparse.sparse_coo_tensor(indices, values, (3, 3)) print("dense:") print(sp.to_dense().data) Save / load a state dict from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn m = nn.Linear(4, 4) sd = m.state_dict() m2 = nn.Linear(4, 4) m2.load_state_dict(sd) print("keys:", list(sd.keys())) Learning-rate warmup + cosine decay import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim, schedulers m = nn.Linear(4, 2) opt = optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=0.01) sched = schedulers.LinearWarmupCosineDecay(opt, total_steps=20, warmup_steps=5) lrs = [] for step in range(8): x = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32)) loss = m(x).sum() loss.backward() opt.step() opt.zero_grad() sched.step() lrs.append(round(float(opt.lr), 6)) print("lr schedule:", lrs) Reproducibility seed import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor np.random.seed(42) a = Tensor(np.random.randn(3).astype(np.float32)) np.random.seed(42) b = Tensor(np.random.randn(3).astype(np.float32)) print("reproducible:", np.allclose(a.data, b.data))

docs.text: Distributed Training Guide SNEPPX-Alg provides production-grade distributed training primitives with NCCL hardware acceleration and deterministic CPU fallbacks. Architecture Overview flowchart TD DDP["Data Parallel (DDP)"] --> Collectives["AllReduce Gradients"] ZeRO1["ZeRO-1"] --> OptState["Shard Optimizer States"] ZeRO2["ZeRO-2"] --> OptGrad["Shard States + Gradients"] ZeRO3["ZeRO-3"] --> OptParam["Shard States + Gradients + Weights"] TP["Tensor Parallel"] --> ColSplit["Matrix Col/Row Partitioning"] PP["Pipeline Parallel"] --> StageSplit["Sequential Layer Partitioning"] DDP (Distributed Data Parallel) DDP replicates model weights on every rank while feeding independent data mini-batches: from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import distributed from SneppX_ALG import Tensor, F, nn, optim # Initialize process group (CPU fallback or NCCL) pg = distributed.init_process_group(world_size=4, rank=0, backend="gloo") model = nn.Linear(64, 16) opt = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) # Inside training loop: all-reduce gradients before optimizer step x = Tensor.randn((8, 64)) loss = model(x).sum() loss.backward() for p in model.parameters(): if p.grad is not None: distributed.all_reduce(p.grad, op="mean") opt.step() opt.zero_grad() ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) Stages Stage What is Sharded Memory Reduction Communication Volume ZeRO-1 Optimizer States ($m, v$) $4\times$ reduction Identical to standard DDP ZeRO-2 Optimizer States + Gradients $8\times$ reduction Identical to standard DDP ZeRO-3 Optimizer States + Gradients + Parameters Linear with rank count $+50\%$ communication overhead Enabling ZeRO in Training Configuration # config/training/distributed.yaml distributed: backend: nccl world_size: 8 zero_stage: 2 gradient_accumulation_steps: 4 all_reduce_bucket_size_mb: 25 Multi-Node Launching via CLI # Single-node multi-process sneppx-train --config config/training/distributed.yaml --world-size 4 --rank 0 # Multi-node launcher invocation sneppx-train --config config/training/distributed.yaml --master-addr 10.0.0.1 --master-port 29500 --world-size 16 --rank 0 CPU Fallback for Local Development When running without multiple GPUs or NCCL drivers, all collective operations ( all_reduce , broadcast , all_gather ) seamlessly execute as local identity operations, guaranteeing that code developed on a laptop runs unchanged on high-performance compute clusters.

docs.text: Getting Started This guide walks you through installing SNEPPX-Alg and running your first training loop. Installation pip install sneppx-alg Or install in development mode from source: git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git cd sneppx-alg pip install -e . To run with local development bindings without installation: $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" First Tensor & Autograd Tensors support automatic differentiation out of the box with tape-based backpropagation: import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor # Create a tensor requiring gradients x = Tensor(np.array([2.0, 3.0, 4.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True) # Forward arithmetic y = (x * x + 3.0 * x).sum() # Backward pass to compute dy/dx y.backward() print("x.grad:", x.grad) # [7.0, 9.0, 11.0] First Neural Network Training Loop import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor, F from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim np.random.seed(0) class MLP(nn.Module): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(4, 8) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(8, 2) def forward(self, x): return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x))) model = MLP() opt = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2) for step in range(200): x = Tensor(np.random.randn(32, 4).astype(np.float32)) y = Tensor((2.0 * x.data[:, :2]).astype(np.float32)) loss = F.mse_loss(model(x), y) loss.backward() opt.step() opt.zero_grad() print("final loss:", round(float(np.asarray(loss.data).reshape(-1)[0]), 4)) Next Steps Autograd Guide — higher-order automatic differentiation, JVP and VJP Distributed Guide — DDP, ZeRO-1/2/3, and tensor parallelism Security Layers — S0–S9 AI framework defense-in-depth Model Zoo Browser — browse supported foundation model architectures

docs.text: Higher-Order Autodiff SNEPPX-Alg supports higher-order differentiation via create_graph=True . Computing Hessians import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True) y = (x ** 2).sum() y.backward(create_graph=True) # x.grad is now a tensor with a graph hessian = (x.grad * x.grad).sum() hessian.backward() Exact Hessian verification The higher-order AD is verified against exact Hessians for: - Linear functions: H = 2 A^T A - Quadratic forms - Conv1d (kernel and input) - LayerNorm, RMSNorm - All loss functions jvp (forward-mode) from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.autograd import jvp def f(x): return x * x x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True) tangent = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])) result = jvp(f, x, tangent) # J @ tangent vjp (reverse-mode) from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.autograd import vjp def f(x): return x * x x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True) cotangent = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])) result = vjp(f, x, cotangent) # grad of dot(cotangent, f(x)) Gradient checkpointing from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.grad_checkpoint import checkpoint def heavy(x): return x * x out = checkpoint(heavy, x) # saves memory Supported ops with create_graph All 40+ ops support create_graph=True : - Arithmetic: Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Pow, MatMul - Activations: ReLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, GELU, SiLU - Norms: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, BatchNorm - Losses: MSE, CrossEntropy, BCE, KLDiv, NLL, SmoothL1, Huber - Conv: Conv1d, Conv2d, Conv3d - Pooling: MaxPool, AvgPool, AdaptiveAvgPool, AdaptiveMaxPool - And more...

docs.text: HSS training guide This guide explains how to build, run, and train a Hierarchical State Space (HSS) model with SNEPPX-Alg, end to end, on CPU. It walks through the autodiff tape, the layer-normalization step, and a minimal training loop. 1. Model and parameters An HSS model is created from a config and a seed: SNEPPXHSSConfig cfg; cfg.state_dim = 4; cfg.input_dim = 4; cfg.output_dim = 4; cfg.num_layers = 1; cfg.seq_len = 1; cfg.dt_min = 0.01f; cfg.dt_max = 0.1f; cfg.use_hierarchical = 0; SNEPPXHSSModel* model = SNEPPX_hss_model_create(&cfg, 42); Per-layer parameters (9 tensors each) are enumerated by SNEPPX_hss_get_params : idx name meaning 0 A state transition 1 B input->state 2 C state->output 3 D feedthrough 4 dt per-step size 5 xp input projection weight 6 xpb input projection bias 7 ng layer-norm gain ( norm_gamma ) 8 nb layer-norm shift ( norm_beta ) 2. Building the training graph Each training step: Wraps the model parameters in SNEPPXVariable* (with requires_grad = 1 ). Builds the forward graph with SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph . Attaches an SNEPPX_mse_loss . Runs SNEPPX_tape_backward . Steps the optimizer (CPU or CUDA-accelerated). Destroys the tape (after nulling the weight data pointers). SNEPPXTape* tape = SNEPPX_tape_create(); SNEPPXVariable** wv = /* SNEPPX_variable_create(pt[i], 1) for each param */; SNEPPXVariable* inv = SNEPPX_variable_create(input, 0); SNEPPXVariable* outv = NULL; SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph(model, tape, inv, wv, nw, &outv); SNEPPXVariable* tgv = SNEPPX_variable_create(target, 0); SNEPPXVariable* loss = SNEPPX_mse_loss(tape, outv, tgv); SNEPPX_tape_backward(tape, loss); SNEPPXTensor** gt = /* wv[i]->grad */; SNEPPX_optimizer_step(opt, pt, gt, nw); 3. The layer-norm step Inside SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph (file algorithms/hss/core/forward_train.c ), each timestep computes: x_col -> xp_out = matmul(xp, xt_col) -> xp_b = add(xp_out, xpb) -> xp_norm = layer_norm(xp_b, ng, nb, 1e-5) <- gain/shift here -> h_new = add(matmul(A_bar, h), matmul(B_bar, xp_norm)) ... SNEPPX_layer_norm stores ctx->gamma = gamma (the variable). Its backward reads the float buffer as c->gamma->data->data (not c->gamma->data ). 4. Optimizer SNEPPXOptimizerConfig opt_cfg = SNEPPX_optimizer_config_default(); opt_cfg.learning_rate = 0.03f; opt_cfg.type = SNEPPX_OPTIMIZER_ADAM; SNEPPXOptimizer* opt = SNEPPX_optimizer_create(&opt_cfg); // Optional: use CUDA-accelerated optimizer SNEPPXTrainConfig train_cfg = SNEPPX_train_config_default(); train_cfg.use_cuda_optimizer = 1; // requires SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON SNEPPX_optimizer_step(opt, params, grads, n) applies the update in place. When use_cuda_optimizer=1 , the trainer transparently transfers params/grads to GPU and runs cuBLAS SGD or AdamW. 5. Verifying training works Run the bundled integration test: cmake --preset release cmake --build build --config Release --target test_train_integration & build\tests\Release\test_train_integration.exe Expected (v0.9.7): init=0.234858 final=0.015788 ratio=0.0672 PASS Loss should drop by >90% over 10 Adam steps. 6. Tips Learning rate: 0.03 with Adam over 10 steps is enough to show convergence. Determinism: fixed seed + Adam => reproducible runs. CUDA optimizer: Enable use_cuda_optimizer for GPU-accelerated optimizer steps. The forward and backward passes remain on CPU. Don't free params via the tape: null wv[i]->data before SNEPPX_tape_destroy so the model's parameter tensors survive across steps.

docs.text: Installation Guide Prerequisites Tool Minimum Version Notes CMake 3.24 Build system (4.x recommended for CUDA) C compiler C11 MSVC 2022, GCC 11+, Clang 14+ C++ compiler C++20 Only needed for S2 obfuscation engine Python 3.11+ Optional (for bindings + test runner) CUDA Toolkit 12.x Optional (for CUDA optimizer, SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON ) Linux Ubuntu / Debian # Install build tools sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y build-essential cmake git # Build git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git cd sneppx-alg cmake --preset release cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc) # Test cd build && ctest --output-on-failure Fedora / RHEL sudo dnf install -y gcc gcc-c++ cmake git # Same build steps as above macOS Intel (x86_64) brew install cmake gcc git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git cd sneppx-alg cmake --preset release cmake --build build -j$(sysctl -n hw.ncpu) cd build && ctest --output-on-failure Apple Silicon (ARM64) brew install cmake git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git cd sneppx-alg cmake --preset release cmake --build build -j$(sysctl -n hw.ncpu) cd build && ctest --output-on-failure Windows Native (Ninja + MSVC) # Open "Developer Command Prompt for VS 2022" git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git cd sneppx-alg cmake --preset release cmake --build build --config Release cd build ctest -C Release --output-on-failure PowerShell Script .\scripts\build.ps1 -Config Release -Tests .\scripts\test.ps1 -Config Release Build Options Option Default Description SNEPPX_BUILD_TESTS ON Build test suite SNEPPX_BUILD_BENCHMARKS ON Build benchmarks SNEPPX_BUILD_PYTHON OFF Build Python bindings SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA OFF Build CUDA kernels (requires CUDA Toolkit 12.x) SNEPPX_USE_ASAN OFF Enable AddressSanitizer SNEPPX_USE_UBSAN OFF Enable UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer SNEPPX_USE_LTO OFF Enable Link-Time Optimization SNEPPX_BUILD_ZK OFF Build zero-knowledge proof backend CMake Presets cmake --list-presets # Available: # debug — Debug build with tests # release — Release build with tests # relwithdebinfo — Release with debug info # ninja-release — Ninja + Release # asan — Debug + AddressSanitizer Python Setup No build needed for pure-Python wrappers: $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" python -c "from SneppX_ALG import *" For C-backed Python (optional): # Requires pybind11 cmake --preset release -DSNEPPX_BUILD_PYTHON=ON cmake --build build --config Release CUDA Setup cmake -B build -G Ninja -DSNEPPX_BUILD_TESTS=ON -DSNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON cmake --build build --config Release Requires CUDA Toolkit 12.x with MSVC integration. Verify Installation # Run full test suite cd build && ctest --output-on-failure # Run specific test ctest -C Release -R test_tensor # Run Python tests $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" python tests/python/test_algo_wrappers.py # Run benchmarks ./tests/benchmark/bench_tensor Troubleshooting Build fails: "cannot open program database" MSVC parallel build issue. The CMakeLists.txt includes /FS flag. If still failing: cmake --build . --config Release -j1 Test fails: "Ed25519 verify" or "Argon2 timing" Pre-existing S0 edge case failures (2/306 Ed25519 vectors, 1/4 Argon2 timing). Not security vulnerabilities. CMake 4.x version error If CMake fails with invalid version string , ensure you have the v1.0.0 tag checked out. Python import fails $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" python -c "import SneppX_ALG; print(SneppX_ALG.__file__)" CUDA not found Ensure CUDA_PATH environment variable is set and points to CUDA Toolkit 12.x.

docs.text: Loss gallery Pick a loss function and see both its value and its gradient . The gradient is what the optimiser actually follows, so two losses that look similar can behave very differently in training. loss Why the gradient matters more than the value Loss Gradient for large error Effect MSELoss grows linearly outliers dominate the update L1Loss constant robust to outliers, but noisy near zero HuberLoss clipped at δ quadratic near zero, linear in the tails SmoothL1Loss → sign(z) same idea, C¹-continuous at ±β log-cosh → ±1, smoothly robust and differentiable everywhere Geman-McClure → 0 bounded influence: very strong outlier rejection HingeLoss 0 once satisfied no gradient for already-correct margins BCEWithLogits → −1 never stops pushing on badly wrong predictions focal loss → 0 for easy examples down-weights well-classified samples quantile loss asymmetric pinball loss for a τ-quantile forecast Robust vs sensitive, side by side import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn pred = Tensor(np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True) tgt = Tensor(np.zeros(4, dtype=np.float32)) mse = nn.MSELoss()(pred, tgt) mse.backward() print("MSE grad:", np.asarray(pred.grad.data)) # outlier at 10 dominates Add an outlier to the target and MSELoss moves the whole batch; L1Loss or HuberLoss barely notice. That is the entire reason those losses exist. import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn pred = Tensor(np.zeros(4, dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True) tgt = Tensor(np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0], dtype=np.float32)) for name, loss_fn in [("L1", nn.L1Loss()), ("Huber", nn.HuberLoss())]: loss = loss_fn(pred, tgt) loss.backward() print(name, "grad:", np.asarray(pred.grad.data)) pred.zero_grad_() Classification losses For a binary problem the logit z is mapped through a sigmoid. Plotting the loss against z shows why BCEWithLogitsLoss is numerically preferred over sigmoid followed by BCELoss : the fused form avoids log(0) when a prediction saturates. import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn logits = Tensor(np.array([-20.0, 0.0, 20.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True) target = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], dtype=np.float32)) loss = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()(logits, target) loss.backward() print("loss:", float(np.asarray(loss.data).reshape(-1)[0])) print("grad:", np.asarray(logits.grad.data)) # saturates to 0 and -1, never NaN See also: Optimizer race · Autograd visualizer · Cookbook .

docs.text: Matmul visualizer Matrix multiplication is a sum of row · column dot products. Hover any cell of C to see exactly which row of A and which column of B produced it — and the arithmetic term by term. A 3×4 × B 4×3 = C 3×3 🎲 Randomize ▶ Sweep all cells Why it matters for training The same shape rule governs linear layers: an input (N, K) times a weight (K, N_out) produces (N, N_out) . A shape mismatch like (N, C, L) @ (C,) fails instead of broadcasting — reshape the bias to (1, C, 1) first, as SNEPPX-Alg's Conv layers do. import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor x = Tensor(np.random.randn(2, 3).astype(np.float32)) w = Tensor(np.random.randn(3, 4).astype(np.float32)) print((x @ w).shape) # (2, 4) — batch dimension preserved See also: Autograd visualizer · Conv2d visualizer · Higher-order AD .

docs.text: Optimizer race Four optimizers, same starting point, same loss surface. Press Start and watch SGD (momentum), Adam , AdamW , and NAdam race to the minimum. surface elliptic bowl Rosenbrock curved valley ▶ Start Reset What to look for Elliptic bowl — high curvature in one direction. SGD with momentum zig-zags; Adam-family methods rescale per-coordinate and cut straight across. Rosenbrock — the classic narrow curved valley. Momentum helps, but plain SGD needs far more steps; adaptive methods follow the valley quickly. AdamW vs Adam — AdamW decouples weight decay, so it drifts slightly less. These are illustrative dynamics (a plain JS implementation of the update rules), not a benchmark of the C engine. For the real implementations see optim.py and Cookbook → learning-rate warmup . import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG import Tensor from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim for name, cls in [("SGD", optim.SGD), ("Adam", optim.Adam), ("AdamW", optim.AdamW), ("NAdam", optim.NAdam)]: m = nn.Linear(4, 2) opt = cls(m.parameters(), lr=1e-2) x = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32)) m(x).sum().backward() opt.step() opt.zero_grad() print(name, "ok") See also: Autograd visualizer · Loss gallery .

docs.text: Post-Quantum Crypto Known-Answer Testing (PQC KAT) — status and write-up 2026-11-13 update. Companion to issue #16 (official NIST ACVP vector harness) in the SneppX/sneppx-alg tracker. The deterministic RNG used by seeded key-generation tests is now compiled only into explicit test builds. What was implemented SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.acvp_kat — a NIST ACVP harness for the C crypto backend ( _SNEPPX_c.crypto ), plus vendored official vectors: tests/data/acvp/*.json . Test suites (availability depends on build configuration): suite tests what it proves tests/python/test_acvp_sha3.py 4 C sha3_256 == NIST official KATs (40 byte-aligned SHA3-256 AFT vectors from SHA3-256-2.0 ), C==hashlib on the same messages, FIPS 202 empty-string KAT tests/python/test_acvp_mlkem.py conditional Deterministic keyGen and encaps/decaps tests require a test-only extension built with SNEPPX_ENABLE_TEST_RNG=ON ; production builds skip this module. No FIPS validation is claimed. tests/python/test_acvp_slhdsa.py conditional Signature-verification vectors and C roundtrip/tamper tests; seeded determinism requires a test-only build. KeyGen vectors are explicitly skipped because they provide no reproducible entropy input accepted by the current C API. tests/python/test_acvp_mldsa.py conditional Signature-verification and roundtrip/tamper tests; deterministic keyGen vectors require a test-only extension built with SNEPPX_ENABLE_TEST_RNG=ON . Vector provenance: usnistgov/ACVP-Server gen-val/json-files/ sample vector sets (NIST, public domain): SHA3-256-2.0 , ML-KEM-keyGen-FIPS203 , ML-KEM-encapsDecaps-FIPS203 , ML-DSA-sigVer-FIPS204 , ML-DSA-keyGen-FIPS204 , SLH-DSA-sigVer-FIPS205 , SLH-DSA-keyGen-FIPS205 . Bit-level vector policy (why SHA3-256 subset is byte-aligned) ACVP msg values are bit strings ( len counts bits , final nibble zero-padded). The finalized SHA-3 approved function pads after the last message bit , so when len % 8 != 0 the digest is not the digest of any byte string: the padding pattern lands mid-byte. Those vectors equal the Keccak Team's ShortMsgKAT_SHA3-256.txt bit-level digests (verified against the published XKCP test-vector file). Neither the C byte-string API nor Python hashlib can absorb bit-level messages, so we vendor byte-aligned ( len % 8 == 0 ) vectors only for autonomous testing. ML-DSA/SLH-DSA sigVer messages are all byte-aligned (or have no msgLen ), so their full sets are vendored. Verifying bit-level KATs would require a bit-length sponge API on the C side; that is the documented follow-up. Honest interop report acvp_kat.interop_report(crypto, vectors, runner) aggregates C-verifier decisions against NIST's testPassed flags. SHA3-256 : 100 % KAT agreement (C digest == NIST md == hashlib on all vendored vectors). ML-KEM (Kyber) : deterministic keygen and encaps/decaps KATs require the test-only RNG hook. That hook is not compiled into production builds. Keygen agreement is measured byte-for-byte against NIST ek / dk ; the implementation remains experimental and is not FIPS validated. ML-DSA & SLH-DSA : invalid foreign signatures are rejected, but valid finalized FIPS signatures are not fully interoperable with the current C wire formats. These implementations remain experimental. Keygen coverage: - ML-KEM keyGen : run_mlkem_keygen() seeds the C test RNG with each vector's d value and compares ek / dk byte-for-byte against FIPS 203 expected values. - ML-DSA keyGen : run_mldsa_keygen() seeds the C test RNG with each vector's seed value and compares pk / sk against FIPS 204 expected values. - SLH-DSA keyGen : explicitly marked unsupported by the harness because the vendored sample set does not provide reproducible entropy inputs that can be passed to the current key-generation API. Those vectors are counted as skipped, not as successful interoperability. The harness reports unsupported suites as skipped. It is a regression and interoperability tool, not a FIPS validation certificate. No invalid signature is accepted by the tested signature-verification paths. How to reproduce $env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python" python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_sha3.py -q -p no:cacheprovider python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_mlkem.py -q -p no:cacheprovider python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_slhdsa.py -q -p no:cacheprovider python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_mldsa.py -q -p no:cacheprovider The _SNEPPX_c extension must be built. Production builds omit deterministic RNG controls. To run seeded key-generation tests, configure a separate test build with -DSNEPPX_ENABLE_TEST_RNG=ON and build the Python extension. Never ship or distribute that test build. Signature-verification tests that do not need deterministic key generation can run against a production extension.

docs.text: Security Architecture Overview SNEPPX-Algo organizes its security work into ten phases (S0-S9), covering cryptography, memory hardening, obfuscation, runtime monitoring, network security, AI sanitization, key management, secure updates, formal verification, and penetration-testing infrastructure. Implementation maturity varies by component: some areas are experimental, partial, or scaffolded. This document describes the intended architecture and current implementation evidence; it is not a security certification or a claim that every control is production-ready. Each phase builds on the previous. The architecture is designed so that security is not a bolt-on layer but a property of the entire system. S0 ── S1 ── S2 ── S3 ── S4 ── S5 ── S6 ── S7 ── S8 ── S9 │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ Crypto Memory Obfusc Monitor Network AI UI Update Formal Pentest Core Secure Engine Engine Sec San Sec Sec Verif Report Mem S0 — Cryptographic Core (experimental) Status : Experimental / partial Source : security/crypto/c/ and include/neural_core/security/ All crypto source files follow the four-layer commenting standard in COMMENTING.md : Layer 1 file headers, Layer 2 concept blocks, Layer 3 inline "why" comments, and Layer 4 Doxygen API docs on every public SNEPPX_* function. docs.text: SNEPPX-Algo organizes its security work into ten phases (S0-S9), covering cryptography, memory hardening, obfuscation, runtime monitoring, network security, AI sanitization, key management, secure updates, formal verification, and penetration-testing infrastructure. Implementation maturity varies by component: some areas are experimental, partial, or scaffolded. This document describes the intended architecture and current implementation evidence; it is not a security certification or a claim that every control is production-ready. Each phase builds on the previous. The architecture is designed so that security is not a bolt-on layer but a property of the entire system. docs.text: Security Layers Deep Dive (S0–S9) S0 — Cryptographic Core Purpose: Experimental cryptographic primitives for signing, encryption, hashing, and key exchange. Presence of an implementation does not establish production readiness, constant-time behavior, certification, or independent review. Components: - Ed25519 (RFC 8032) signatures: historical documentation reports 304/306 vectors passing; current vector coverage must be reconciled before claiming full conformance - X25519 (RFC 7748) key exchange: Full DH exchange - ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439) AEAD: encrypt/decrypt - SHA-3 (FIPS 202): 224/256/384/512 - SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4): General-purpose hashing - BLAKE3: Fast hashing - Argon2id (RFC 9106): KDF implementation; historical timing tests reported platform-dependent variation - Secure Random: OS CPRNG (Windows CNG / Linux getrandom) - Kyber-512/768/1024 (FIPS 203 ML-KEM): PQ key encapsulation - Dilithium-2/3/5 (FIPS 204 ML-DSA): PQ digital signatures - SPHINCS+-128/192/256 (FIPS 205 SLH-DSA): Stateless PQ signatures Files: security/crypto/c/ PQC ACVP status: Official NIST ACVP sample vectors are vendored under tests/data/acvp/ and exercised through SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.acvp_kat . Coverage is partial, not a claim of FIPS validation or certification: SHA3-256 vectors match; ML-KEM key-generation and encapsulation/decapsulation checks are present; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA currently reject invalid signature vectors but do not yet verify all valid finalized FIPS signatures because their C wire formats remain pre-finalization. See docs/pqc_kat.md for the interop report and limitations. Treat PQC support as experimental until those gaps are closed and independently reviewed. S1 — Memory Hardening Purpose: Runtime memory protection against corruption, leakage, and exploitation. Components: - Guard pages: Inaccessible pages placed before/after heap allocations - Stack canaries: Random values on stack, checked before function return - ASLR: Random base addresses for heap/mmap allocations - Locked memory: mlock() / VirtualLock to prevent swapping of secrets - Secure wipe: memset with compiler barrier (prevents optimizer removal) - Constant-time comparison: Timing-attack-resistant memcmp - Memory leak detector: Tracks allocations, reports unfreed blocks Files: security/memory/ S2 — Obfuscation Engine Security warning: The S2 audit records unresolved RNG, timing-side-channel, code-transformation, and memory-safety findings. Do not rely on obfuscation as a security boundary or as protection for secrets. See the detailed audit . Purpose: Protect against reverse engineering and static analysis. Components: - Control flow flattening: switch-based dispatch replaces natural control flow - String encryption: XOR-based compile-time obfuscation with rotating keys - Instruction substitution: NAND-gate equivalent sequences - Opaque predicates: always-true/false branches - Code virtualization: basic-block bytecode with encrypted dispatch table - Anti-debug: ptrace, NtGlobalFlag, timing anomaly, breakpoint scanning - Binary substitution: opcode-level replacement with prefix/suffix bytes - Junk code insertion: NOP slides, dead-store MOVs, identity XORs - Constant unfolding: integer constants as (a + b) with random splits - IAT protection: hash-based import resolution, integrity scanning - SEH/VEH obfuscation: exception-based control flow - TLS callback obfuscation: runtime function pointer encoding - Anti-dump: PE/ELF header XOR encryption with CRC integrity - Multi-VM diversity: multiple bytecode handlers with slot switching - Instruction scheduling randomization: basic-block-level reordering Files: security/cpp/ , security/obfuscation/ S3 — Behavioral Monitor Purpose: Runtime monitoring and anomaly detection for security events. Components: - Integrity monitoring: CRC32-based memory region verification - Container breakout detection: cgroup/namespace/mount inspection - Frequency analysis: unusual API call pattern detection - Timing analysis: side-channel probing via rdtsc measurement - Anomaly detection: statistical baseline comparison for runtime behavior Files: security/monitor/ S4 — Network Security Purpose: Protect network communication against attacks. Components: - DDoS mitigation: SYN flood detection, rate limiting, connection tracking, IP blacklisting - Transport security: TLS handshake padding, traffic analysis resistance - Identity management: certificate pinning, peer fingerprint verification - Certificate validation: chain-of-trust with expiry checking Files: security/network/ S5 — AI Sanitizer Purpose: Protect model from adversarial inputs and data poisoning. Components: - Prompt injection detection: regex + embedded pattern scanning - Differential privacy: Laplace mechanism with configurable epsilon - Data poisoning defense: gradient outlier detection, loss spike monitoring - RLHF safety: reward model validation, preference alignment, harmful output filtering - Output verifier: constraint checking against allow/deny lists Files: security/ai/ S6 — Security UI / Key Vault Purpose: Secure key management and audit logging. Components: - Audit logging: structured JSON entries with severity, timestamps, source - Key vault: in-memory encrypted key store with PIN-protected access Files: security/ui/ S7 — Secure Updates Purpose: Ensure software updates are authentic and tamper-proof. Components: - Container security: OCI layer verification, manifest integrity, image signing - Signed update bundles: Ed25519-signed payloads (signature over BLAKE3 update hash) with version rolling - Rollback protection: monotonic version/min-version checks preventing downgrade attacks - Staged rollout: gradual distribution with health-check gating Status notes: SNEPPX_update_verifier_check is fail-closed when no trusted public key is configured and verifies Ed25519 signatures against the configured trusted key. Production key provisioning, trust distribution, and rollout policy remain review items (see maturity notes in README). Files: security/updates/ S8 — Formal Verification Purpose: Mathematical guarantees of critical algorithm properties (bounded/pragmatic). Components: - Model checking: bounded state-space exploration for critical paths - Invariant verification: pre/post-condition checking on memory safety - LTL/safety checks: bounded safety-oriented handling (e.g., deadlock-oriented properties); unsupported/full LTL formulas are not claimed as verified - State reduction: SNEPPX_model_minimize performs reachable-state reduction (not full bisimulation minimization) Status notes: S8 provides bounded, fail-closed-oriented checks for supported properties; it is not a complete formal proof system for all LTL/properties. Files: security/formal/ S9 — Penetration Testing Purpose: Proactive security assessment and vulnerability discovery. Components: - Network fuzzer: protocol-aware engine with mutation strategies - Self-audit: comprehensive internal consistency checks - Security report generation: structured output of audit findings - CTF utilities: challenge scaffolding for red-team exercises Files: security/pentest/ Threat Model Assumptions: - Hardware is trusted (no side-channel attacks on CPU) - OS is trusted (no kernel-level compromise) - Network is untrusted - Other AI models are untrusted and potentially adversarial - Supply chain is trusted (verified commits, signed releases) Defenses: Threat Defense Signature forgery Ed25519 Data breach at rest ChaCha20-Poly1305 Side-channel timing Constant-time ops Memory scraping Locked memory + guard pages Swap forensic mlock / VirtualLock Reverse engineering CF flattening + string encryption Runtime tampering Behavioral monitor Adversarial input ARC input guard + adversarial training Gradient leakage ARC gradient obfuscation Model inversion ARC output verifier Reporting: algoSNEPPX@gmail.com See security.md for the security overview and security/ for threat modeling docs.

docs.text: Sparse Tensors SNEPPX-Alg supports sparse tensors in COO, CSR, CSC, and BSR formats. Creating sparse tensors import numpy as np from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.sparse import sparse_coo_tensor, sparse_csr_tensor # COO format indices = np.array([[0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2]]) values = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) sp = sparse_coo_tensor(indices, values, (3, 3)) Dense interop dense = sp.to_dense() sparse = dense.to_sparse() Sparse operations from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.sparse import sparse_mm, sparse_addmm # Sparse @ dense result = sparse_mm(sparse_tensor, dense_matrix) # Sparse @ sparse result = sparse_mm(sparse_a, sparse_b) Layouts Strided — dense (default) SparseCOO — coordinate format SparseCSR — compressed sparse row SparseCSC — compressed sparse column SparseBSR — block sparse row SparseAdam optimizer from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.optim import SparseAdam opt = SparseAdam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) SparseAdam handles sparse gradients efficiently by updating only non-zero entries.

docs.text: Code Walkthrough — ARC (Adversarial Robustness Certification) ARC is the third stage of the SNEPPX-Alg pipeline. It hardens the model against adversarial inputs by combining three defense mechanisms: an input guard, gradient obfuscation, and output verification. It also simulates adversarial attacks (FGSM/PGD) so the model can be adversarially trained. Public header: include/neural_core/architecture/adversarial_robustness_certification.h Implementation: algorithms/arc/core/ CUDA extensions: algorithms/arc/cuda/ Configuration SNEPPXARCConfig cfg = SNEPPX_arc_config_default(); cfg.input_guard_strength = 0.1f; cfg.gradient_obfuscation_method = SNEPPX_OBF_NOISE; // NONE|NOISE|CLAMP|MIXED cfg.gradient_noise_scale = 1e-4f; cfg.gradient_clip_max = 1.0f; cfg.output_verify_layers = 2; cfg.output_verify_threshold = 0.95f; cfg.adversarial_training = 1; cfg.attack_simulation_types = SNEPPX_ATTACK_FGSM | SNEPPX_ATTACK_PGD; cfg.attack_epsilon = 0.01f; The three defense mechanisms An ARC layer ( SNEPPXARCLayer ) is composed of three sub-objects: 1. Input guard ( SNEPPXInputGuard ) SNEPPX_arc_input_guard_forward(guard, input, &sanitized, &anomaly_score) projects the input onto a learned subspace ( projection_matrix ) and scores how anomalous it is against training statistics ( norm_stats_mean / var ). Anomalous samples are sanitized before they reach the rest of the model. 2. Gradient obfuscator ( SNEPPXGradientObfuscator ) SNEPPX_arc_obfuscate_gradients(obf, gradients, method) hides gradient signal from attackers during training. Four methods: Method Behavior SNEPPX_OBF_NONE no modification SNEPPX_OBF_NOISE add Gaussian noise (scale gradient_noise_scale ) SNEPPX_OBF_CLAMP clip to gradient_clip_max SNEPPX_OBF_MIXED noise + clamp 3. Output verifier ( SNEPPXOutputVerifier ) SNEPPX_arc_verify_output(verifier, output, &verified_output, &confidence) runs the output through a small verification network and checks consistency against a history of recent outputs. Low-confidence or inconsistent outputs are corrected before being returned. Attack simulation SNEPPX_arc_simulate_attack(clean_input, attack_type, epsilon, &adversarial) generates adversarial examples: SNEPPX_ATTACK_FGSM — one-step sign-gradient perturbation. SNEPPX_ATTACK_PGD — iterative projected gradient descent. SNEPPX_ATTACK_CW — Carlini–Wagner style attack (declared; bit flag 4). Attack types are bit flags, so SNEPPX_ATTACK_FGSM | SNEPPX_ATTACK_PGD enables both. Forward and adversarial training The plain forward pass: SNEPPXARCLayer* layer = SNEPPX_arc_layer_create(&cfg, input_dim, output_dim, seed); float security_metrics = 0.0f; SNEPPX_arc_forward(layer, input, &output, &security_metrics); security_metrics aggregates the guard's anomaly score, obfuscation activity, and verifier confidence so callers can monitor defensive posture. Two training graphs exist: // Standard graph: input -> guard -> obfuscated training int rc = SNEPPX_arc_build_train_graph(layer, tape, input_var, weight_vars, num_weights, &output_var); // Adversarial graph: builds BOTH clean and adversarial branches so the // loss can combine clean accuracy with robustness. int rc2 = SNEPPX_arc_build_adversarial_train_graph(layer, tape, input_var, weight_vars, num_weights, &clean_output, &adv_output); Minimal example #include "adversarial_robustness_certification.h" SNEPPXARCConfig cfg = SNEPPX_arc_config_default(); cfg.attack_epsilon = 0.05f; SNEPPXARCLayer* layer = SNEPPX_arc_layer_create(&cfg, 8, 8, 42); SNEPPXTensor* clean = /* build (4, 8) input */; SNEPPXTensor* adv = NULL; SNEPPX_arc_simulate_attack(clean, SNEPPX_ATTACK_PGD, 0.05f, &adv); SNEPPXTensor* out = NULL; float sec = 0.0f; SNEPPX_arc_forward(layer, adv, &out, &sec); SNEPPX_arc_layer_destroy(layer); Public API summary Lifecycle: SNEPPX_arc_config_default , SNEPPX_input_guard_create/destroy , SNEPPX_gradient_obfuscator_create/destroy , SNEPPX_arc_output_verifier_create/destroy , SNEPPX_arc_layer_create/destroy . Defense: SNEPPX_arc_input_guard_forward , SNEPPX_arc_obfuscate_gradients , SNEPPX_arc_verify_output , SNEPPX_arc_forward . Attacks: SNEPPX_arc_simulate_attack . Training: SNEPPX_arc_get_params , SNEPPX_arc_build_train_graph , SNEPPX_arc_build_adversarial_train_graph .

docs.text: Code Walkthrough — FM (Fractal Memory Orchestrator) FM is the fifth and final stage of the SNEPPX-Alg pipeline. It manages distributed, federated memory: a network of nodes, each with its own memory bank, that periodically synchronize their knowledge. FM also compresses gradients, adds privacy noise, and protects against catastrophic forgetting. Public header: include/neural_core/architecture/fractal_memory_orchestrator.h Implementation: algorithms/fm/core/ CUDA extensions: algorithms/fm/cuda/ Configuration SNEPPXFMConfig cfg = SNEPPX_fm_config_default(); cfg.num_nodes = 8; // participating nodes/ranks cfg.memory_dim = 512; // width of each memory entry cfg.memory_capacity = 10000; // entries per bank cfg.sync_interval = 100; // steps between syncs cfg.sync_method = SNEPPX_SYNC_ALL_REDUCE; // ALL_REDUCE|GOSSIP|TOPOLOGY cfg.compression_ratio = 0.25f; // fraction of gradients transmitted cfg.privacy_epsilon = 1.0f; // DP noise budget cfg.catastrophic_forgetting_protection = 1; cfg.ewm_alpha = 0.05f; // exponential moving average decay Memory bank SNEPPXFMMemoryBank is an associative key-value store over tensors: SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_create(memory_dim, capacity) SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_write(bank, key, value) — upsert by key SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_read(bank, key) — lookup by key SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_forget(bank, forget_rate) — age out stale entries using access_counts / timestamps Nodes and controller A node ( SNEPPXFMNode ) pairs a memory bank with a gradient accumulator, liveness state, last-sync timestamp, and a trust_score . The controller ( SNEPPXFMController ) owns all nodes plus a shared sync state ( global_memory , sync_round , node_contributions , conflict_log ). SNEPPXFMController* ctrl = SNEPPX_fm_controller_create(&cfg); SNEPPXTensor* out = NULL; int rc = SNEPPX_fm_forward(ctrl, node_id, input, &out); FM has no trainable parameters of its own — SNEPPX_fm_get_params returns 0 and SNEPPX_fm_build_train_graph is a pass-through ( input_var → output_var ). Synchronization algorithms/fm/core/sync.c implements three sync strategies: Method Function Pattern All-reduce SNEPPX_fm_sync_all_reduce ring/butterfly all-reduce of memory deltas NCCL SNEPPX_fm_sync_nccl pluggable callback ( SNEPPXFMSyncCallback ) for a real NCCL process group Gossip SNEPPX_fm_sync_gossip randomized pairwise exchange Topology SNEPPX_fm_sync_topology fixed neighbor graph sync Gradient exchange helpers: SNEPPX_fm_send_gradients / SNEPPX_fm_receive_gradients . Compression, privacy, forgetting Compression : SNEPPX_fm_compress_gradients(gradients, ratio) top-k sparsifies gradients. Error feedback (EF-SGD) : SNEPPX_fm_error_feedback_create(dim, ratio) + SNEPPX_fm_compress_with_error(ef, gradient) accumulate the compression error so the top-k selection stays accurate across steps. Privacy : SNEPPX_fm_add_privacy_noise(data, epsilon) adds calibrated Gaussian noise for (ε)-differential privacy. Forgetting : SNEPPX_fm_ewm_update(bank, alpha) applies an exponential moving average to bank entries so old knowledge decays gradually instead of being overwritten. Adaptive sync : SNEPPX_fm_compute_change_rate(bank, new_values) + SNEPPX_fm_adaptive_sync_interval(ctrl, base_interval) shrink the sync interval when memory changes rapidly and lengthen it when it is stable. docs.text: FM is the fifth and final stage of the SNEPPX-Alg pipeline. It manages distributed, federated memory: a network of nodes, each with its own memory bank, that periodically synchronize their knowledge. FM also compresses gradients, adds privacy noise, and protects against catastrophic forgetting. Public header: include/neural_core/architecture/fractal_memory_orchestrator.h Implementation: algorithms/fm/core/ CUDA extensions: algorithms/fm/cuda/
docs.title: Code Walkthrough — FM (Fractal Memory Orchestrator)

docs.text: SNEPPXFMMemoryBank is an associative key-value store over tensors: SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_create(memory_dim, capacity) SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_write(bank, key, value) — upsert by key SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_read(bank, key) — lookup by key SNEPPX_fm_memory_bank_forget(bank, forget_rate) — age out stale entries using access_counts / timestamps
docs.title: Memory bank

docs.text: A node ( SNEPPXFMNode ) pairs a memory bank with a gradient accumulator, liveness state, last-sync timestamp, and a trust_score . The controller ( SNEPPXFMController ) owns all nodes plus a shared sync state ( global_memory , sync_round , node_contributions , conflict_log ). SNEPPXFMController* ctrl = SNEPPX_fm_controller_create(&cfg); SNEPPXTensor* out = NULL; int rc = SNEPPX_fm_forward(ctrl, node_id, input, &out); FM has no trainable parameters of its own — SNEPPX_fm_get_params returns 0 and SNEPPX_fm_build_train_graph is a pass-through ( input_var → output_var ).

docs.text: algorithms/fm/core/sync.c implements three sync strategies: Method Function Pattern All-reduce SNEPPX_fm_sync_all_reduce ring/butterfly all-reduce of memory deltas NCCL SNEPPX_fm_sync_nccl pluggable callback ( SNEPPXFMSyncCallback ) for a real NCCL process group Gossip SNEPPX_fm_sync_gossip randomized pairwise exchange Topology SNEPPX_fm_sync_topology fixed neighbor graph sync Gradient exchange helpers: SNEPPX_fm_send_gradients / SNEPPX_fm_receive_gradients .

docs.text: Compression : SNEPPX_fm_compress_gradients(gradients, ratio) top-k sparsifies gradients. Error feedback (EF-SGD) : SNEPPX_fm_error_feedback_create(dim, ratio) + SNEPPX_fm_compress_with_error(ef, gradient) accumulate the compression error so the top-k selection stays accurate across steps. Privacy : SNEPPX_fm_add_privacy_noise(data, epsilon) adds calibrated Gaussian noise for (ε)-differential privacy. Forgetting : SNEPPX_fm_ewm_update(bank, alpha) applies an exponential moving average to bank entries so old knowledge decays gradually instead of being overwritten. Adaptive sync : SNEPPX_fm_compute_change_rate(bank, new_values) + SNEPPX_fm_adaptive_sync_interval(ctrl, base_interval) shrink the sync interval when memory changes rapidly and lengthen it when it is stable.

docs.text: Code Walkthrough — HSS (Hierarchical State Space) HSS is the first stage of the SNEPPX-Alg pipeline. It maps input sequences to a latent state using a recurrent state-space model (SSM) inspired by structured state-space sequence models such as Mamba/S6. Public header: include/neural_core/architecture/hierarchical_state_space.h Implementation: algorithms/hss/core/ CUDA extensions: algorithms/hss/cuda/ The model An HSS model is a stack of layers, each with a recurrent state and a set of SSM parameters: Field Meaning A state transition matrix B input → state projection C state → output projection D feedthrough (skip) term dt per-step sampling interval x_proj , x_proj_bias input projection (input_dim → 2·state_dim) h the current recurrent state A_bar , B_bar discretized (ZOH or bilinear) versions of A and B norm_gamma , norm_beta per-layer normalization parameters Configuration SNEPPXHSSConfig cfg = SNEPPX_hss_config_default(); cfg.state_dim = 64; // latent state width per layer cfg.input_dim = 512; // input feature width cfg.output_dim = 512; // output feature width cfg.num_layers = 2; cfg.seq_len = 1024; cfg.dt_min = 0.001f; cfg.dt_max = 0.1f; cfg.use_hierarchical = 1; // multi-resolution state levels cfg.use_parallel_scan = 1; // associative scan instead of loop SNEPPX_hss_config_default() returns state_dim=64, input/output 512, 2 layers, seq_len 1024, and hierarchical + parallel scan enabled. Forward path The forward pass is the sequence of calls in algorithms/hss/core/forward.c : SNEPPX_hss_discretize(layer) — converts continuous (A, B, dt) into the discrete (A_bar, B_bar) used for step-by-step recurrence. Two underlying methods exist: SNEPPX_hss_discretize_zoh() — zero-order hold. SNEPPX_hss_discretize_bilinear() — bilinear (Tustin) transform. SNEPPX_hss_scan(layer, x_seq, h_seq, y_seq) — sequential scan over the input sequence, computing hidden states h_t and outputs y_t step by step. SNEPPX_hss_parallel_scan(layer, x_seq, h_seq, y_seq) — associative-scan variant that computes the same recurrence in parallel (much faster on long sequences). Used when use_parallel_scan is set. SNEPPX_hss_hierarchical_scan(layer, x_seq, y_seq) — multi-resolution scan used when use_hierarchical is set. The state space is decomposed into SNEPPX_hss_hierarchical_levels(state_dim, min_dim) coarse-to-fine levels. The public entry point is: SNEPPXHSSModel* model = SNEPPX_hss_model_create(&cfg, seed); int rc = SNEPPX_hss_forward(model, input_tensor, &output_tensor); SNEPPX_hss_step(layer, x, h_next) performs a single-token recurrent update and is used for autoregressive generation. Training graph Training uses the autodiff framework: SNEPPXTape* tape = /* created by the trainer */; SNEPPXVariable* input_var, **weight_vars; SNEPPXVariable* output_var; int rc = SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph(model, tape, input_var, weight_vars, num_weights, &output_var); Parameters are flattened in a fixed order by SNEPPX_hss_get_params() (see the 9-parameter table in hss_training.md ). Minimal example #include "hierarchical_state_space.h" SNEPPXHSSConfig cfg = SNEPPX_hss_config_default(); cfg.state_dim = 4; cfg.input_dim = 4; cfg.output_dim = 4; cfg.num_layers = 1; cfg.seq_len = 8; SNEPPXHSSModel* model = SNEPPX_hss_model_create(&cfg, 42); SNEPPXTensor* in = /* build (8, 4) input tensor */; SNEPPXTensor* out = NULL; SNEPPX_hss_forward(model, in, &out); SNEPPX_hss_model_destroy(model); Public API summary Lifecycle: SNEPPX_hss_config_default , SNEPPX_hss_layer_create/destroy , SNEPPX_hss_model_create/destroy . Discretization: SNEPPX_hss_discretize , SNEPPX_hss_discretize_zoh , SNEPPX_hss_discretize_bilinear . Recurrence: SNEPPX_hss_step , SNEPPX_hss_scan , SNEPPX_hss_parallel_scan , SNEPPX_hss_hierarchical_scan , SNEPPX_hss_hierarchical_levels . Inference: SNEPPX_hss_forward . Training: SNEPPX_hss_get_params , SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph .
